b: Today we welcome Andrew Foy to add his opinion!
Today’s prompt is: What makes a great clinical teacher? We have all had them, and maybe identifying what made them great will help us in our practice or train more great educators.

A great clinical teacher is first and foremost a role model of clinical excellence. Within the invaluable setting of a longitudinal relationship, a great clinical teacher demonstrates what it truly means to be a good doctor. Trainees learn by watching an attending prepare thoroughly and treat every patient with warmth, patience, and respect. By practicing active listening, shared decision-making, and jargon-free communication, the clinician demonstrates how to build and maintain a strong therapeutic relationship.

Beyond role modeling, a great clinical teacher cultivates psychological safety. Medicine is intimidating, and learners who fear humiliation or sense an oppressive hierarchical structure will stay silent. They won’t ask questions. They won’t take chances in making a diagnosis or offering a management plan. They will stay stuck in a reporter mode and shy away from questioning, and taking chances to show their thinking. A great teacher empowers learners to speak up and grow without fear.

To bridge the gap between novice and expert, a great teacher makes their clinical reasoning visible. Experienced doctors often rely on rapid pattern recognition, which can seem like magic to trainees. A skilled educator slows down to narrate their thought process aloud, explaining how patient history and test results shift probabilities or why a standard guideline might not fit a complex case. Just as importantly, they model intellectual humility alongside their up-to-date expertise by openly admitting when they do not know something and looking it up together.

Finally, effective clinical teachers tailor their mentorship to the learner’s developmental stage. They help medical students build foundational frameworks and gather accurate histories. For residents, they step back to grant graduated autonomy, offering targeted feedback to sharpen clinical triage. For fellows, they shift from supervisor to colleague, debating nuances of clinical practice, especially critical appraisal of the literature, to prepare them for independent practice and lifelong learning.
Ultimately, a great clinical teacher shapes trainees into physicians whom he or she would want to care for themself or family members in the future.
The most memorable teacher in my career was former president of the ACC Dr. Suzanne Knoebel.
When she was your attending at the VA in Indianapolis, it was like playing for your toughest coach. Everyone was at their best lest she would tell you that you failed the patient.

Her brand of teaching was to expect you knew everything about the patient; his symptoms, exam findings, labs, x rays and past admissions. Dr Knoebel knew we were learners so she didn’t expect us to be masters of cardiology, but she did expect us to be masters of the patient’s case.

Modern medical practice—with its shift work, frequent hand-offs and radiologists reading from home—are nearly opposite to her brand of uber-accountability. I’m doing hospital consults this holiday week and I am struck by the incredible complexity of in-patients. I go room to room thinking that I hope some highly competent person is running the show. You see this in surgeons; they tend to stay engaged as the commander-who knows-everything-about-the-patient. but, too often, on the medical service, no one takes the commander role. It changes with the days.

Though we rounded together decades ago, I remember like it was yesterday, Dr Knoebel telling me that you did not have to be a genius to be a good doctor, you just had to work hard at not missing important things about the patient. You had to care enough not to miss things. Honestly, this is 90% of good care. I am afraid that AI may not substitute for such a committed accountable commander.
I've had so many great teachers. I divide them into those I learned from in person and those I learned from through their writing and online lectures.

What unites all of them is that they genuinely understand what they are teaching. I believe the number one error people make when teaching is that they do not actually understand the topic. They may have a very superficial knowledge of that topic.

You may think this is rare. But it is incredibly common. You could find a GI oncologist who has practiced for 15 years at one of the top cancer centers in America. And they can certainly tell you how they treat a 49-year-old patient with metastatic rectal cancer. But that's not teaching. Teaching is explaining why they do things the way they do, and why they don't do it in a different manner. Many experts struggle because they haven't thought through it enough.
The best clinical teachers also have a temperament and personality that is well suited for the job.

Meanwhile, I've learned a lot from people remotely. When I started in medicine, and discovered a scientist I liked, I would read all their articles and essays. You came to recognize their tone, and broader philosophy of medicine. I put John Ioannidis and Rita Redberg and Allen Brett and Gil Welch and Peter Gotszche others in this bucket.

I’ve been lucky enough to have a pretty diverse set of great clinical teachers. There have been people who didn't even know my name but served as role models, and great teachers who were more colleagues than teachers. Four qualities stand out.

Great clinical teachers respect the practice of medicine. This might seem hopelessly old-fashioned, but I still see medicine as a vocation. My great clinical teachers recognized the specialness of the practice of medicine. They knew that we practice only for the good of a patient and that although we strive to do our best, perfect practice is impossible. My teachers left me dedicated to and in awe of our mission.

Great clinical teachers are experts. Yes, we want doctors to recognize that they can’t know everything and that they are fallible humans, but that we should still demand and expect excellence. I have respected and admired my teachers’ knowledge; I learned facts from them and was inspired to achieve their level of mastery.

Great clinical teachers are transparent in their thinking. To confer knowledge, teachers need to let learners into their heads. They say that Ted Williams couldn’t teach people to hit because it came so naturally to him. I have met great doctors, people who make the diagnostic process look easy, who cannot explain how they do it. You might want one of these people as your doctor; you do not want one of them as your teacher. Usually, exposing the thought process lets the student in on content knowledge as well as ways to handle uncertainty.

Lastly, great clinical teachers are invested in their students. Medical education should always center around mentored clinical activity. Facts can be gleaned from a book or webpage, but the practice of medicine can only be taught by a doctor at the bedside. Because medicine is so hard to learn, trainees need teachers invested in both the practice and the student.
